outcome: Still open in general. Since 26 Jan 2024 it has gained computer-assisted proofs for 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13 runners (2025-26, arXiv and one journal paper), and two unreviewed 2026 preprints by one author claim 14 and 15 runners; no source records a general result, and several single-author or AI-linked claims of a complete proof sit unvetted.
problem_asks: (1) For every number k of runners (k >= 2, all k) with pairwise distinct constant speeds on a unit-length circular track, all starting together at time 0. (2) Each runner is, at some time, at distance at least 1/k from every other runner (lonely). The conjecture is one universal claim over all k; no list of finite cases answers it. Convention: the frozen wording counts runners, so k runners with threshold 1/k are the same claim as k-1 nonzero speeds with threshold 1/k in the literature's indexing (Wills-Cusick; Epoch and the 2025-26 papers use k speeds with 1/(k+1)). 'Eight runners' in Rosenfeld's title is the k=8 instance in the frozen wording and k=7 speeds in the literature. The frozen statement asks nothing else (no reduction, no bound, no counterexample search).

events.what_happened: Small cases settled by Betke and Wills in 1972. Wikipedia's history table lists the four-runner case for 1972; a 2025 survey summary in the search index (not opened) says the case k <= 3 (four runners) was settled by Betke and Wills in 1972. The primary paper was not opened.
events.delivers: The conjecture for at most four runners (three nonzero speeds). Restricted to that count.
events.remains: Five or more runners, and the claim for all k.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for the smallest counts.

events.delivers: A small case (four or five runners; the count is disputed across sources), with computer assistance.
events.remains: Larger counts, and the claim for all k.
events.direction: Confirms the conjecture for a small count.

Published in the Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 33(1) P1.38 on 27 Feb 2026.

events.what_happened: Malikiosis, Santos and Schymura, 'Linearly-exponential checking is enough for the Lonely Runner Conjecture and some of its variants', arXiv:2411.06903 (v1 11 Nov 2024; v2 21 Jun 2025). Reduces the finite check: velocities up to C(n+1,2)^{n-1}, at most n^{2n}, suffice (improving Tao's n^{O(n^2)}). Same bound for the shifted conjecture, with a dependence on a Lonely Vector Problem. In dimension two they reprove the shifted conjecture for four runners; in dimension three the shifted case for five runners reduces to speed sets summing to 195.

Its own runner-count results are for the shifted variant (four runners in dimension two; five-runner reduction in dimension three).
events.remains: The classical conjecture for every n, and the claim for all k.

events.what_happened: Zenodo record 16936620, 'LLM Math case Study: A Proof of the Lonely Runner Conjecture via the Minimal Inertia Principle and Information Geometry' (v1, 24 Aug 2025; a newer version exists and was not read). The record states: 'This paper presents a complete proof of the conjecture for all real speeds.' The argument, as the abstract describes it: a Minimal Inertia Principle for rationally dependent speeds, an information-geometric Covariance Inequality, and an extension to all real speeds by a closedness argument. The authors are Miroku Akagi and Yumeto Kokuno (the record lists them as 'Miroku, Akagi and Kokuno, Yumeto'; the companion record lists them in the reverse order).
events.revisions: v1 24 Aug 2025; a newer version is noted on the record and was not read.

events.remains: Nothing, if the claim is correct; no reviewed record exists.
events.doubts: The record states the work was 'performed in significant part by AI' and names no system. The record shows no affiliation, no community reviews and no comments. The authors' companion Zenodo record (16929436, 22 Aug 2025, 'The Deductive Capacity of Large Language Models in Mathematical Research') carries the note '[This is a creative exploration of a concept with AI -it should not be taken as correct mathematics.]' and a correction dated 5 Aug 2026 that declares its own GPT-5 Pro diagnosis wrong and supersedes it with DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17010427. That companion concerns a different problem (gradient descent), so it is a track-record signal only.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture holds (every runner lonely), for all speeds.

Proves the conjecture for eight runners (seven nonzero speeds, threshold 1/8) by computer verification, using recent results that bound the size of a minimal counterexample. The abstract says the approach also covers the known cases of four to seven runners and that minor improvements might reach nine or ten. The intro calls the conjecture 'a well-known open problem'. The implementation is in a LIRMM GitLab repository.

Proves a polynomial improvement on the best lower bound for maximum loneliness: ML(V) >= 1/(2n) + 1/n^{5/3+o(1)} for any n distinct positive integers (Theorem 1.3), against earlier forms 1/(2n) + c/n^2 and Tao's 1/(2n) + (log n)^{1-o(1)}/n^2. The paper remarks that if the conjecture is true this bound would be optimal.

Theorem 1.3: LRC(k) holds for k <= 12, i.e. for 11, 12 and 13 runners, by a computer-assisted proof that refines the sieving framework of Rosenfeld and Trakulthongchai, with lifting, modulo-p symmetry and a polynomial-method argument (Proposition 1.4) for speed tuples modulo odd primes. Concluding remarks include a heuristic reduction (Proposition 7.1) that the authors do not use for Theorem 1.3.

events.what_happened: Lee, 'Lonely runners in real life: Sharp bounds for time-dependent velocities', arXiv:2607.16082 (v2 stamped 24 Jul 2026; a search summary gives 27 Jul). Studies a variant with locally integrable time-dependent velocities: the slowest and fastest runners are each eventually at least 2^{-n+1} from all others, which is optimal, and intermediate runners can be held arbitrarily close to another runner. Its Conjecture 1.1 is the classical constant-speed conjecture, which the paper calls 'notoriously difficult', says is known only for n <= 13, and says 'remains widely open'.

events.direction: Concerns a different question (time-dependent velocities). Its own status statement for the classical conjecture is that it is open, known for n <= 13.

events.what_happened: Zhang, 'Tight instances of the Lonely Runner Conjecture: complete classification of one-entry modifications, a new infinite family, and the growth bound', arXiv:2608.13599 (v1 1 Aug 2026; v2 31 Aug 2026). Classifies one-entry modifications of {1,...,n-1} whose maximum loneliness equals the conjectured 1/n (tight sets), finds a new infinite family, proves an n log n growth bound for tight one-entry modifications, and reports a computer census for n <= 140. It treats the conjecture as the reference value and is stated conditionally on it.
events.delivers: Results about extremal (tight) configurations for sets of n-1 speeds. Does not establish the conjecture for any n.
events.remains: The conjecture for every n, and the claim for all k. The paper's own statement is conditional on the conjecture.

The same result is the first version of arXiv:2609.02604, titled 'Fourteen lonely runners', submitted 2 Sep 2026.

events.what_happened: Beck and Everett, 'Lonely Runner Relations', arXiv:2609.06259 (v1 5 Sep 2026; v2 23 Sep 2026). A structural reduction: any counterexample or tight instance of the conjecture has a nonzero integer vector m with bounded 1-norm (at most min(2k+3, ((k+1)/(k-1)) flt(k)), flt(k) Khinchin's flatness constant) orthogonal to the speed vector, so potential counterexamples lie in finitely many hyperplanes. Generalises to shifted runners and recovers Czerwinski (2012) for random n.
events.delivers: A reduction for the classical conjecture (potential counterexamples lie in finitely many hyperplanes). No runner count is settled.
events.remains: The conjecture for every n, and the claim for all k.

disputes.summary: Who was first on the nine-runner case. arXiv shows Trakulthongchai's nine-and-ten paper first (v1 27 Nov 2025) and Rosenfeld's nine-runner paper second (v1 1 Dec 2025). Rosenfeld's preprint says Trakulthongchai 'independently announced' a proof a couple of days before its submission. Quanta says Rosenfeld 'independently proved the nine-runner case a few days later'. The sources describe the sequence differently; no winner is chosen here.

Historical small-case attributions conflict. Wikipedia: four runners 1972 (Betke and Wills); five runners 1984 (Cusick and Pomerance, computer-assisted); six runners 2001 (Bohman, Holzman and Kleitman); seven runners 2008 (Barajas and Serra). Search summaries: Cusick and Pomerance did four runners in 1984; Bienia et al. gave a simpler four-runner proof in 1998; Bohman, Holzman and Kleitman did five runners in 2001, with Renault (2004) a shorter proof. Quanta: four runners in the 1970s and seven by 2007. These differences look like a one-runner counting convention, and the primary papers were not opened.

Wikipedia's lead (last edited 28 Aug 2026 per its footer) says the conjecture is 'known to be true for 13 runners or fewer'. That predates the fourteen- and fifteen-runner preprints of Sep 2026, so the page is out of date on the present record. Epoch's benchmark page says 'known to be true for n <= 12' in its own convention (n speeds), which is the same as 13 runners.

The sLRC small-case statements conflict. Blanco, Criado and Santos give shifted-conjecture counterexamples starting at n = 5 (arXiv 2603.24784). A 2025 paper by Alcantara, Criado and Santos is said (search summary, not opened) to prove the shifted conjecture for five runners. The indexing convention (runners versus generators or dimension) may account for the difference; not resolved.

The fourteen- and fifteen-runner computations are described by the same author in two places that disagree on AI. The arXiv paper (2609.02604, current version) has a section 'Data availability and use of artificial intelligence' disclosing LLM assistance. The Zenodo records (22066772, 22667683) mention no AI. Whether arXiv v1 (2 Sep 2026, titled 'Fourteen lonely runners') carried the disclosure was not checked.

The author order for the 2025 Zenodo LLM record differs from its companion record: 'Miroku, Akagi and Kokuno, Yumeto' on record 16936620, and 'Yumeto Kokuno and Akagi Miroku' on record 16929436. Presented here as the records show them.

summary:
The conjecture is still open in general. Every 2026 source read says so: the Quanta article (6 Mar 2026), the 2026 preprints' own introductions, Epoch's benchmark page, Wikipedia's lead, ProofAtlas's status page, and the Perarnau-Serra survey (arXiv 2409.20160, first posted 30 Sep 2024, last revised Aug 2025, 'still widely open'). What has moved since 26 Jan 2024 is the verified finite range, by computer-assisted case proofs: eight runners (Rosenfeld, arXiv Sep 2025); nine and ten (Trakulthongchai, arXiv Nov 2025, EJC 5 Jun 2026); nine (Rosenfeld, arXiv Dec 2025); eleven to thirteen (Sungkawichai and Trakulthongchai, arXiv Apr 2026, preprint); fourteen (Allikvere, Zenodo 23 Aug 2026) and fifteen (Allikvere, Zenodo 9 Sep 2026; combined arXiv 2609.02604). The fourteen- and fifteen-runner results are single-author, unreviewed, and in one case only self-audited. Bedert (arXiv Nov 2025) moved the best general lower bound on maximum loneliness from 1/(2n) + c/n^2 to 1/(2n) + 1/n^{5/3+o(1)}, which is a bound move on the named quantity and still short of the conjectured value. Malikiosis, Santos and Schymura (Nov 2024; Forum of Mathematics, Sigma 2025) reduce the finite check to velocities at most n^{2n}; that changes no runner count for the classical statement. Variants: Blanco, Criado and Santos (Mar 2026) disprove the shifted conjecture from n = 5 and the Lonely Vector Property from n = 12; Fan and Sun (arXiv 2023; EJC Feb 2026) disprove the Loneliness Spectrum Conjecture for n = 4; Poliakova (Sep 2026) quantifies shifted failure; Lee (Jul 2026) treats time-dependent velocities; Beck and Everett (Sep 2026) give a finite-hyperplane reduction. Unvetted complete-proof claims: Zenodo 16936620 (Akagi, Kokuno, 24 Aug 2025), which states 'This work was performed in significant part by AI' and names no system; Zenodo 19171253 (bhaskar kumar, 22 Mar 2026, elementary, unaffiliated); and the Runtolap GitHub repository, whose own labels say '(fake) no proof'. A GitHub issue (SzymonPawlus/...#297, 11 Sep 2026, labels 'agent:codex', Claude named as reviewer) is labelled as an agent campaign on the fifteen-runner case and says 'It is not solved'. Searches for a lab announcement or AI-benchmark result on this problem found none; Epoch lists the conjecture as an open FrontierMath problem with no recorded AI attempt.

AI involvement, as the sources state it. Named systems in result-bearing text: 'OpenAI GPT-5' assisted code generation for the nine- and ten-runner computations (Trakulthongchai, EJC 2026), with the sieve method credited to the author; 'ChatGPT-5.6 Pro' is credited with a proof sketch of Proposition 7.1 in the concluding remarks of the eleven-to-thirteen-runner preprint, which Theorem 1.3 does not use. Unnamed AI: 'AI-based tools' for the eleven-to-thirteen code (the authors say 'the process was closely supervised' and 'the code was manually verified'); LLMs for code development, drafting, exploring proof ideas and error search in the fourteen-and-fifteen paper (the authors say 'No model output is treated as mathematical evidence'); 'generative AI' for a single generalisation step in Lee's variant paper; 'performed in significant part by AI' in the 2025 Zenodo claim. The eight- and nine-runner papers have no AI disclosure in the full text read. The repository for the eleven-to-thirteen code contains a log script described as 'entirely AI generated' and 'for sanity check only'; this is repository-level, not in the preprint text. An early search-summary claim about an LLM disclosure in the fourteen-and-fifteen paper was confirmed against its full text; the summary's other specifics were not relied on.

Close calls. (1) The fifteen-runner date: the arXiv v1 of 2 Sep 2026 claims only fourteen, so the fifteen-runner first public written argument is dated 9 Sep 2026 from the Zenodo record; a reader who takes the combined arXiv version as the first public argument would move it to 2 Sep, and would also make the fourteen-runner event coincide with it. (2) Whether AI-written verification code is 'in the result': the authors of the nine- and ten-runner paper say the mathematics is theirs and the AI wrote optimisation code; the computation is the proof, so this is contestable. (3) Whether the Zenodo 2025 'AI in significant part' claim is load-bearing: its proof text was not read, so what the AI produced cannot be stated. (4) Counting convention: a 'k runners, threshold 1/k' statement and a 'k speeds, threshold 1/(k+1)' statement are the same claim, and sources differ by one in which count is 'known'. (5) The Wikipedia status ('13 or fewer') predates the Sep 2026 preprints, so it does not reflect them.
competing_reading: A reader who counts only finitely many instances of a universal claim as moving nothing (the Collatz test in the brief) could say the eight-to-fifteen-runner results are a finite census and should not be read as progress on the problem. The reply is that each runner count is a restricted class of the statement (infinitely many speed sets for a fixed n), and the brief says a case settled counts. Second reading: the Bedert bound and the Malikiosis-Santos-Schymura reduction are the only in-window events that move a named quantity or a general method, so they are the clearer 'bound moved' events, while the runner-count results are case settlements. Third reading: the unvetted complete-proof claims (2025 Zenodo, 2026 Zenodo, Runtolap) could be treated as events of a lower evidential standard, not as events at all; the record keeps them because the brief says to record discounted claims, and their discounting is for the judging pass.
what_would_settle_it: For the fourteen- and fifteen-runner results: an independent rerun of the gate certificates, or a referee report. For the Zenodo and GitHub 'complete proof' claims: a public mathematical review, or the PDF text (the Zenodo 2026 PDF and the Dogra PDF were not readable here). For the AI attributions: the authors' statement naming the model and the step it produced, in the 2025 Zenodo record and in the fourteen-and-fifteen paper (which says 'large language models' without naming one). For the counting convention: a qualified reader confirming which statement the bullet asks for (k runners with threshold 1/k, equivalently k-1 speeds with threshold 1/k). For the shifted-conjecture conflict: the Alcantara-Criado-Santos paper and the indexing in Blanco et al.

event.what_happened: Rosenfeld, 'The lonely runner conjecture holds for eight runners', arXiv:2509.14111 (v1 17 Sep 2025; v2 16 Oct 2025). Proves the conjecture for eight runners (seven nonzero speeds, threshold 1/8) by computer verification, using recent results that bound the size of a minimal counterexample. The abstract says the approach also covers the known cases of four to seven runners and that minor improvements might reach nine or ten. The intro calls the conjecture 'a well-known open problem'. The implementation is in a LIRMM GitLab repository.
event.revisions: v1 17 Sep 2025; v2 16 Oct 2025 (current). No journal reference on the arXiv record; a search snippet's 'to appear in Mathematics of Computation' was not confirmed.
event.delivers: The conjecture for eight runners. Restricted to that count.
event.remains: Nine or more runners, and the claim for all k.

judgement.why: The statement is one universal claim over all k, so each fixed runner count is a case: there are infinitely many speed sets for each k, so it is not a finite instance check. The 2025-26 computer-assisted proofs for 8 to 15 runners are therefore cases. Only Trakulthongchai's paper is digested, through its EJC publication. The others are unreviewed. The computations are not simple enough to count as checkable. Allikvere's 14- and 15-runner claims are kept but marked doubtful because they rest only on his own audit. Bedert's improvement to the loneliness gap is a bound. The Malikiosis-Santos-Schymura and Beck-Everett papers are reductions and score none. The shifted, spectrum and time-dependent papers are variants. The three complete-proof claims of 2025-26 (two on Zenodo, one PDF on personal storage) are not credible. Runtolap labels itself fake and Kurganskyy withdrew his proof, so both are knocked down. On AI: GPT-5 wrote optimisation code for the verification (F12: coding assistance, so none). ChatGPT-5.6 Pro gave a sketch of Proposition 7.1, a heuristic that Theorem 1.3 does not use, so none. The Codex/Claude issue established nothing. The Akagi-Kokuno record names no system and its ai.systems is empty.
judgement.doubts: The GPT-5 call is the closest one. The verification code is the proof's computation, but by the authors' account the AI wrote low-level optimisation code and the mathematics is their own, so I answered none. Runtolap and the Vance repository have no visible date, so their after_snapshot is null.
